transitivity: both — transitive (click the blue button), intransitive (click on the link)
gloss: To press a mouse button, or to tap a link or icon on a screen.
examples: *Click* the blue button to start the download.
She *clicked* on the wrong link and the page froze.
He kept *clicking* the icon, but nothing happened.
contrast: You click ON a link or simply click a button - both are standard. Click AT is wrong.

transitivity: both — transitive (type your password), intransitive (she types fast)
gloss: To write something on a keyboard.
examples: *Type* your password and press Enter.
He *typed* the whole report in one evening.
She was *typing* an email when the power went out.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: typing, not typeing.

transitivity: both — transitive (scroll the page), intransitive (scroll to the bottom)
gloss: To move text or images up, down, or sideways on a screen.
examples: *Scroll* to the bottom of the page to accept the terms.
I *scrolled* through her photos for twenty minutes.
He has been *scrolling* on his phone all morning.

gloss: To make the picture on a screen look closer or farther away.
examples: Tap the screen twice to *zoom*.
She *zoomed* in on the license plate.
The lens keeps *zooming* by itself.

transitivity: both — transitive (open the app), intransitive (the file opens slowly)
gloss: To make a file, app, or window appear on a screen so you can use it.
examples: *Open* the app and sign in with your email.
I *opened* the attachment and my laptop froze.
The file is *opening* - give it a second.
contrast: No doubled n: opened, opening. The stress is on the first syllable, so the consonant stays single.

transitivity: both — transitive (close the window), intransitive (the app closed by itself)
gloss: To make a file, window, or program stop being open.
examples: *Close* the other tabs to speed up the browser.
He *closed* the laptop without saving the file.
The app keeps *closing* on its own.
contrast: The verb ends in a z sound (KLOHZ). The adjective close, meaning near, ends in an s sound (KLOHS).

gloss: To shrink a window down to the taskbar without closing it.
examples: *Minimize* the window instead of closing it.
She *minimized* the chat and went back to her spreadsheet.
He was *minimizing* every window one by one.
contrast: American spelling uses -ize: minimize, minimized. British writing has minimise.

ru: разворачивать, развернуть (окно на весь экран); максимизировать
gloss: To make a window fill the whole screen.
examples: *Maximize* the video before the call starts.
He *maximized* the window and the text got bigger.
I have *maximized* both windows and they still overlap.

gloss: To make a picture or a window bigger or smaller.
examples: *Resize* the photo before you upload it.
She *resized* the logo to fit the header.
I am *resizing* the window so both files fit.

gloss: To put text or an image you have copied into a new place.
examples: Copy the link and *paste* it into the chat.
He *pasted* the code into the wrong file.
She has *pasted* the same paragraph twice.
contrast: Paste rhymes with taste. You paste something INTO a document.

gloss: To remove a file, a message, or a piece of text for good.
examples: *Delete* the old backups to free up space.
I *deleted* the message by accident.
Someone has *deleted* the whole folder.

gloss: To wipe data off a disk, a phone, or a recording so that nothing is left.
examples: *Erase* the drive before you sell the laptop.
The update *erased* all my settings.
He is *erasing* the old recordings one by one.
contrast: Delete removes one file; erase usually means clearing a whole disk or recording.

gloss: To give a file, folder, or account a new name.
examples: *Rename* the file before you send it.
She *renamed* the folder 'Taxes 2025'.
They have *renamed* the app twice this year.

transitivity: both — transitive (edit the photo), intransitive (she edits for a living)
gloss: To change a text, photo, or video in order to improve or correct it.
examples: You can still *edit* the message for fifteen minutes.
He *edited* the video on his phone.
She has been *editing* the same paragraph all day.
contrast: One t: edited, editing. The stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled.

gloss: To mark text or an item on a screen so that it stands out.
examples: *Highlight* the whole paragraph and press Delete.
She *highlighted* three lines in yellow.
The app is *highlighting* every spelling mistake.
contrast: The gh is silent in both halves of the word: HY-lyt.

ru: добавлять в закладки, добавить в закладки
gloss: To save a web page so that you can find it again quickly.
examples: *Bookmark* this page - you will need it later.
I *bookmarked* the recipe and lost the link anyway.
He has *bookmarked* about four hundred articles.

ru: отмечать, отметить (на фото, в посте); помечать тегом
gloss: To mark a photo, post, or file with a name or a keyword.
examples: Please do not *tag* me in those photos.
She *tagged* her sister in the post.
He is *tagging* every picture with the date.
contrast: Double the g: tagged, tagging.

gloss: To put something into a document, a slot, or a place in a text.
examples: *Insert* the card and wait for the beep.
She *inserted* a chart on the second slide.
He has *inserted* the wrong image again.
contrast: The verb is in-SURT; the noun insert is IN-surt.

gloss: To make an exact second copy of a file, a slide, or a record.
examples: *Duplicate* the slide and change the title.
The script *duplicated* every contact in my phone.
She is *duplicating* the folder as a backup.
contrast: The verb ends in -kayt (DOO-pluh-kayt); the noun and adjective end in a schwa (DOO-pluh-kuht).

gloss: To look at something before it is sent, printed, or published.
examples: *Preview* the email before you hit send.
I *previewed* the file and the formatting was broken.
She is *previewing* the slides on the big screen.

gloss: To cut the edges off a photo so that only part of it is left.
examples: *Crop* the photo so the trash can is not in the shot.
She *cropped* the picture into a square.
He is *cropping* the screenshots before he posts them.
contrast: Double the p: cropped, cropping.

transitivity: both — transitive (refresh the page), intransitive (the feed refreshes every minute)
gloss: To load the newest version of a page or a feed.
examples: *Refresh* the page and the error should be gone.
I *refreshed* the tracking page every five minutes.
The app is *refreshing* your inbox.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -sh: refreshes.

transitivity: both — transitive (reload the page), intransitive (the page reloaded by itself)
gloss: To load a page or a file again.
examples: *Reload* the page if the video will not play.
The browser *reloaded* and lost everything I had typed.
It has been *reloading* for two minutes.

transitivity: both — transitive (toggle the setting), intransitive (toggle between the two views)
gloss: To switch a setting on or off, or to move back and forth between two options.
examples: *Toggle* dark mode in the settings menu.
He *toggled* the switch and the screen went black.
She was *toggling* between two spreadsheets all morning.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: toggling.

transitivity: both — transitive (download the file), intransitive (the update is downloading)
gloss: To copy a file from the internet onto your own device.
examples: *Download* the app from the official store.
I *downloaded* the update last night.
The movie is still *downloading*.
contrast: Download brings a file TO your device; upload sends it FROM your device.

transitivity: both — transitive (upload the photos), intransitive (the video is uploading)
gloss: To copy a file from your device to the internet.
examples: *Upload* your ID to finish the application.
She *uploaded* the video at three in the morning.
Twelve photos have been *uploaded* so far.

gloss: To make a file smaller so that it takes less space or sends faster.
examples: *Compress* the folder before you email it.
He *compressed* the video and lost some quality.
The app is *compressing* two hundred photos.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -ss: compresses.

gloss: To put files into a single compressed folder.
examples: *Zip* the folder and send it over.
She *zipped* the files and mailed them to the client.
He is *zipping* the whole project directory.
contrast: Double the p: zipped, zipping.

gloss: To open a compressed folder and take the files out.
examples: *Unzip* the file before you run the installer.
I *unzipped* the archive and found nothing inside.
The program is *unzipping* the backup now.
contrast: Double the p: unzipped, unzipping.

gloss: To pull files or data out of an archive or a larger set.
examples: *Extract* the folder to your desktop.
The tool *extracted* every email address from the page.
It is *extracting* three thousand files.
contrast: The verb is ik-STRAKT; the noun extract (a short passage) is EK-strakt.

gloss: To move messages or files into storage instead of deleting them.
examples: *Archive* the thread - do not delete it.
She *archived* every email from last year.
He has *archived* the whole folder by mistake.
contrast: Archiving keeps the file and hides it; deleting removes it.

gloss: To prepare a disk for use by erasing it, or to arrange the look of a text.
examples: *Format* the drive before you install the system.
He *formatted* the wrong disk and lost his photos.
She is *formatting* the report to match the template.
contrast: Double the t: formatted, formatting, even though the stress is on the first syllable.

gloss: To turn data into code so that only the right person can read it.
examples: *Encrypt* the folder before you put it in the cloud.
The app *encrypted* the messages end to end.
All of our backups are *encrypted*.

gloss: To turn coded data back into a readable form.
examples: Only the key can *decrypt* the file.
They *decrypted* the message in under an hour.
The program is *decrypting* the archive now.

transitivity: both — transitive (sync your contacts), intransitive (the phone syncs at night)
gloss: To make two devices or accounts hold the same up-to-date data.
examples: *Sync* your phone with the laptop.
The calendar *synced* and the old events came back.
My photos have not been *syncing* since Tuesday.
contrast: Sync sounds exactly like sink. Keep the c in the forms: synced, syncing. You sync one device WITH another.

gloss: To list and organize data so that it can be searched quickly.
examples: Search engines *index* millions of pages a day.
Google *indexed* the new site within a week.
The database is still *indexing*.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -x: indexes.

gloss: To ask a database or a system for particular information.
examples: You can *query* the database straight from the browser.
He *queried* the server and got an empty result.
The script is *querying* three tables at once.
contrast: Consonant + y, so the y changes: queries, queried. The -ing form keeps it: querying.

gloss: To store data for a short time so that it loads faster the next time.
examples: Browsers *cache* images to save time.
The page was *cached*, so I saw yesterday's price.
The app is *caching* the whole playlist.
contrast: Cache is pronounced exactly like cash, not ka-SHAY.

gloss: To put a video, a map, or a piece of code inside a page or a document.
examples: You can *embed* the video right in the post.
She *embedded* a map on the contact page.
He is *embedding* the font in the file.
contrast: Double the d: embedded, embedding.

gloss: To record events or data in a list as they happen.
examples: The app *logs* every failed login attempt.
The system *logged* the error at 2:14 a.m.
The watch has been *logging* our route all day.
contrast: Double the g: logged, logging. Log in and log out are separate phrasal verbs with their own meanings.

gloss: To turn recorded speech into written text.
examples: The app can *transcribe* an hour of audio in a minute.
She *transcribed* the whole interview by hand.
The meeting is being *transcribed* automatically.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: transcribing.

transitivity: both — transitive (dictate a message), intransitive (he dictates instead of typing)
gloss: To speak so that a person or a device writes your words down.
examples: You can *dictate* the text instead of typing it.
He *dictated* the whole email while driving.
She was *dictating* notes into her phone.

gloss: To turn paper documents, photos, or tapes into computer files.
examples: The library wants to *digitize* every old map.
We *digitized* the family videos last summer.
They have been *digitizing* records since 2019.
contrast: American -ize; British writing has digitise.

transitivity: both — transitive (disconnect the drive), intransitive (my phone keeps disconnecting)
gloss: To break the link between a device and a network or another device.
examples: *Disconnect* the drive before you pull the cable.
The call *disconnected* after two minutes.
My laptop keeps *disconnecting* from the Wi-Fi.
contrast: You disconnect FROM a network.

transitivity: both — transitive (reconnect the printer), intransitive (the call reconnected on its own)
gloss: To join a device or a call back to a network after it was cut off.
examples: Try to *reconnect* to the other network.
He *reconnected* the printer and it worked again.
The app is *reconnecting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (pair the headphones with your phone), intransitive (the watch paired in seconds)
gloss: To link two devices over Bluetooth so that they work together.
examples: *Pair* the headphones with your laptop first.
The speaker *paired* on the first try.
My watch is *pairing* right now.
contrast: Pair sounds exactly like pear. You pair one device WITH another.

ru: отключать от сети, отключить; выдёргивать из розетки
gloss: To pull a plug or a cable out of a socket or a device.
examples: *Unplug* the router for ten seconds.
Someone *unplugged* the monitor.
He is *unplugging* every cable to find the bad one.
contrast: Double the g: unplugged, unplugging.

transitivity: both — transitive (recharge the battery), intransitive (the case recharges in an hour)
gloss: To fill a battery with power again.
examples: *Recharge* the battery overnight.
I *recharged* the headphones in the car.
The power bank is *recharging*.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -ge: recharges.

gloss: To supply a device with the electricity it needs to run.
examples: Two small batteries *power* the whole sensor.
The old model was *powered* by a wall adapter.
One cable is *powering* both screens.
contrast: Power up and power down are separate phrasal verbs.

transitivity: both — transitive (switch the setting), intransitive (we switched to a new provider)
gloss: To change from one thing, setting, or service to another.
examples: *Switch* the phone to airplane mode.
We *switched* to a cheaper carrier last year.
She is *switching* between four browser tabs.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: switches. You switch TO a new plan and switch FROM the old one.

transitivity: both — transitive (boot the machine from a USB drive), intransitive (the laptop boots in ten seconds)
gloss: To start a computer so that the operating system loads.
examples: The old tower takes a full minute to *boot*.
He *booted* the laptop from a USB stick.
The machine is still *booting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (reboot the router), intransitive (the server rebooted overnight)
gloss: To start a computer or device again after shutting it down.
examples: *Reboot* the router and try again.
I *rebooted* the laptop three times.
The server is *rebooting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (restart the app), intransitive (the phone restarted by itself)
gloss: To stop a program or a device and start it again right away.
examples: *Restart* the app after the update.
She *restarted* the computer and the error disappeared.
It has been *restarting* for five minutes.

transitivity: both — transitive (stream a movie), intransitive (the video streams in HD)
gloss: To send or watch video or music over the internet while it plays.
examples: We *stream* everything now - no discs in the house.
They *streamed* the whole concert live.
He has been *streaming* the game to two thousand people.

ru: вести прямую трансляцию, транслировать в прямом эфире
transitivity: both — transitive (livestream the ceremony), intransitive (she livestreams every Friday)
gloss: To broadcast an event over the internet while it is happening.
examples: They *livestream* every home game.
She *livestreamed* the wedding for relatives abroad.
He is *livestreaming* from the parking lot.
contrast: Written as one word or as live-stream; both are common. The first part rhymes with five, not with give.

transitivity: both — transitive (the player buffers a few seconds of video), intransitive (the stream keeps buffering)
gloss: To load part of a video or a song in advance so that it plays without stopping.
examples: A weak connection makes every video *buffer*.
The stream *buffered* twice during the final.
It keeps *buffering* right at the good part.

gloss: To respond slowly, so that the picture or the sound falls behind.
examples: The video will *lag* on this connection.
The audio *lagged* about half a second behind.
My screen is *lagging* badly today.
contrast: Double the g: lagged, lagging.

transitivity: both — transitive (transmit the data), intransitive (the beacon transmits every hour)
gloss: To send data or a signal from one place to another.
examples: The sensor can *transmit* data over a mile.
The station *transmitted* the warning at noon.
The device has been *transmitting* all night.
contrast: Double the t: transmitted, transmitting - the stress falls on the last syllable.

gloss: To send data, calls, or traffic along a particular path.
examples: The system *routes* every call through one server.
They *routed* the traffic around the damaged cable.
It is *routing* my request to the wrong office.
contrast: Most Americans say ROOT, like the root of a tree; ROWT is also heard. The -ing form keeps the e: routing.

transitivity: both — transitive (ping me when you land), intransitive (the phone pings all day)
gloss: To send a short signal or message to a device or a person.
examples: *Ping* me when the file is ready.
I *pinged* the server and got no answer.
My phone has been *pinging* every two minutes.

gloss: To show the picture from one screen on another, or to keep an identical copy of data.
examples: You can *mirror* your phone to the TV.
He *mirrored* the laptop screen onto the projector.
The second drive is *mirroring* everything in real time.

gloss: To throw an image from a device onto a screen or a wall.
examples: *Project* the slides onto the white wall.
She *projected* the video from her laptop.
They are *projecting* the game on the side of the building.
contrast: The verb is pruh-JEKT; the noun project is PRAH-jekt.

ru: раздавать интернет с телефона, использовать телефон как модем
transitivity: both — transitive (tether the laptop to your phone), intransitive (we tethered all week)
gloss: To connect a computer to the internet through a phone's data connection.
examples: You can *tether* the laptop to your phone.
He *tethered* for a week while the cable was out.
She is *tethering* from her phone right now.
contrast: You tether one device TO another.

gloss: To remove a program from a computer or a phone.
examples: *Uninstall* the app and install it again.
I *uninstalled* three games to free up space.
It is *uninstalling* the old version now.
contrast: The base already ends in -ll, so the forms look heavy but are regular: uninstalled, uninstalling.

gloss: To install a program or a system again after removing it.
examples: *Reinstall* the driver and reboot.
He *reinstalled* the whole operating system.
She has *reinstalled* the app twice today.

ru: понижать версию, понизить; переходить на более дешёвый тариф
transitivity: both — transitive (downgrade the software), intransitive (we downgraded to the free plan)
gloss: To move to a lower, cheaper, or older version of software or a plan.
examples: You can *downgrade* the plan at any time.
He *downgraded* to the free account.
They are *downgrading* the software to last year's build.
contrast: The opposite of upgrade. Drop the -e before -ing: downgrading.

ru: отлаживать, отладить; искать и исправлять ошибки
transitivity: both — transitive (debug the code), intransitive (he debugs all day)
gloss: To find and fix the errors in a program.
examples: It takes longer to *debug* the code than to write it.
She *debugged* the payment form in one afternoon.
He has been *debugging* the same function for days.
contrast: Double the g: debugged, debugging.

transitivity: both — transitive (compile the program), intransitive (the code compiles cleanly)
gloss: To turn written code into a program that a computer can run.
examples: The code will not *compile* with that typo.
He *compiled* the app for both phones.
It is still *compiling*.

gloss: To run a program or carry out a command.
examples: The server will *execute* the script at midnight.
The command *executed* without an error.
The program is *executing* the last step now.

gloss: To put new software onto the servers where people will use it.
examples: We *deploy* on Thursdays, never on Fridays.
They *deployed* the fix an hour after the outage.
The team is *deploying* the new version tonight.
contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so nothing changes: deploys, deployed. Compare carry - carries - carried.

transitivity: both — transitive (render the video), intransitive (the page renders badly on old phones)
gloss: To turn data or code into a finished image, page, or video.
examples: This laptop cannot *render* 4K video.
The page *rendered* without any styling.
The scene has been *rendering* for six hours.

gloss: To make drawings or objects appear to move on a screen.
examples: You can *animate* the logo in two clicks.
She *animated* the chart so the bars grow.
He is *animating* the intro this week.

gloss: To use a computer to copy the way something works in real life.
examples: The program can *simulate* a whole flight.
They *simulated* the crash a thousand times.
The lab is *simulating* next week's storm.

gloss: To make one system behave exactly like another.
examples: This app can *emulate* an old game console.
The software *emulated* Windows well enough to run the program.
It is *emulating* a printer that no longer exists.

gloss: To work out a result by calculation, usually with a machine.
examples: The server can *compute* the route in a second.
The model *computed* a ninety percent chance of rain.
It is *computing* the totals for all fifty states.

gloss: To change something so that it works as well or as fast as possible.
examples: *Optimize* the images or the page will crawl.
They *optimized* the app for older phones.
He has been *optimizing* the database all week.
contrast: American -ize; British writing has optimise.

transitivity: both — transitive (scale the image), intransitive (the service scales to millions of users)
gloss: To change something in size, or to grow so as to handle much more work.
examples: The design has to *scale* to any screen size.
They *scaled* the service to ten million users.
The company is *scaling* faster than it can hire.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: scaling.

transitivity: both — transitive (integrate the two systems), intransitive (the app integrates with your calendar)
gloss: To make two systems work together as one.
examples: The app can *integrate* with your calendar.
They *integrated* the payment system last month.
We are *integrating* the two databases.
contrast: Integrate WITH another system, or integrate one thing INTO another.

gloss: To put a plan, a rule, or a feature into working form.
examples: They will *implement* two-factor login next quarter.
The team *implemented* the change in one week.
We have *implemented* every fix on the list.
contrast: As a verb the last syllable is full: IM-pluh-ment. The noun, meaning a tool, ends in a schwa: IM-pluh-muhnt.

gloss: To set up a device or a program so that it works the way you want.
examples: *Configure* the printer before you leave.
He *configured* the router for the whole office.
She is *configuring* the new laptops.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: configuring.

gloss: To change settings or content so that they fit one particular person.
examples: You can *personalize* the home screen.
The store *personalized* every email with my name.
The app is *personalizing* your feed.

gloss: To build a rough first version of a product in order to test the idea.
examples: We can *prototype* the app in a week.
They *prototyped* three different layouts.
She is *prototyping* the checkout screen.

gloss: To create new methods, ideas, or products.
examples: Small teams often *innovate* faster than big ones.
The company *innovated* early and took the market.
They have been *innovating* in battery design for years.

ru: писать скрипт, написать скрипт; автоматизировать скриптом
gloss: To write a short program that makes a task run automatically.
examples: You can *script* the whole backup.
He *scripted* the report so that it runs every Monday.
She is *scripting* the tests now.

ru: получать доступ, получить доступ; заходить, зайти (в систему)
gloss: To open or reach data, a file, or an account.
examples: You can *access* the files from any device.
Someone *accessed* my account from another country.
He is *accessing* the server remotely.
contrast: The verb takes a direct object: access the file. Only the noun takes to: access to the file.

transitivity: both — transitive (authenticate the user), intransitive (the device authenticates in a second)
gloss: To prove that a user or a device is who it claims to be.
examples: The app will *authenticate* you with your fingerprint.
The system *authenticated* the login in a second.
It is *authenticating* your device now.

gloss: To check that data or a document is correct and acceptable.
examples: The form will *validate* the email address.
The system *validated* the card and charged it.
It is *validating* the file against the template.

transitivity: both — transitive (lock the screen), intransitive (the phone locks after a minute)
gloss: To stop something from being used or changed without a key, a code, or a password.
examples: *Lock* your screen when you leave the desk.
He *locked* the file so that nobody could edit it.
The phone is *locking* itself every thirty seconds.

gloss: To open something that was locked, or to make a hidden feature available.
examples: *Unlock* the phone with your face.
She *unlocked* the front door from the app.
Finishing the level has *unlocked* two new maps.

gloss: To make a service, a card, or a feature start working.
examples: *Activate* the SIM card before your flight.
He *activated* the alarm from his phone.
They are *activating* the new accounts today.

gloss: To turn off an account or a feature so that it stops working.
examples: You can *deactivate* the account without deleting it.
She *deactivated* her profile for a month.
He is *deactivating* the old key cards.

gloss: To turn a setting or a feature on.
examples: *Enable* two-factor login in the settings.
I *enabled* notifications and now the phone never stops.
Location sharing has been *enabled* by default.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: enabling.

gloss: To turn a setting or a feature off.
examples: *Disable* the pop-ups and the site is readable.
He *disabled* the camera in the settings.
The update has *disabled* my printer.

transitivity: both — transitive (hack an account), intransitive (he learned to hack at fourteen)
gloss: To break into a computer system or an account without permission.
examples: Nobody can *hack* an account with a strong password.
Someone *hacked* the company's mail server.
My account has been *hacked* twice this year.

transitivity: both — transitive (spam the group chat), intransitive (they spam all day)
gloss: To send someone a lot of unwanted messages.
examples: Please do not *spam* the group chat.
They *spammed* every address on the list.
He is *spamming* the comments with links.
contrast: Double the m: spammed, spamming.

gloss: To stop a person, a number, or a site from reaching you.
examples: You can *block* the number in two taps.
She *blocked* him on every app.
The filter is *blocking* half of my mail.

ru: выключать звук, выключить звук; отключать уведомления
gloss: To turn off the sound of a device, a call, or a conversation.
examples: *Mute* yourself when you are not speaking.
He *muted* the group chat for a week.
She is *muting* every notification before bed.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: muting.

gloss: To turn the sound back on.
examples: *Unmute* yourself - we cannot hear you.
He *unmuted* the call and his dog was barking.
She has *unmuted* the thread.

gloss: To stop receiving emails or content from a service you signed up for.
examples: *Unsubscribe* at the bottom of the email.
I *unsubscribed* from forty newsletters in one evening.
He has *unsubscribed* and the mail still keeps coming.
contrast: You unsubscribe FROM a list.

gloss: To mark a message or an item so that it gets attention or review.
examples: *Flag* the email so that you see it later.
The filter *flagged* the message as spam.
Moderators are *flagging* hundreds of posts a day.
contrast: Double the g: flagged, flagging.

ru: писать сообщение, написать сообщение; отправлять сообщение
transitivity: both — transitive (message me the address), intransitive (they messaged back and forth all night)
gloss: To send someone a written message on a phone or an app.
examples: *Message* me when you get there.
She *messaged* him twice and got no answer.
They have been *messaging* since Monday.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: messaging.

transitivity: both — transitive (dial the number), intransitive (dial slowly)
gloss: To enter a phone number in order to make a call.
examples: *Dial* the extension after the beep.
He *dialed* the wrong number twice.
She is *dialing* in from the airport.
contrast: American English keeps one l: dialed, dialing. British writing has dialled, dialling.

transitivity: both — transitive (google the address), intransitive (just google and see)
gloss: To look something up on the internet with a search engine.
examples: *Google* it before you call support.
I *googled* the error message and found the fix.
He was *googling* her name the whole flight.
contrast: As a verb it is written in lowercase, and the -e is dropped: googling.

transitivity: both — transitive (surf the web), intransitive (he surfed for hours)
gloss: To move from page to page on the internet with no fixed goal.
examples: They *surf* the web instead of working.
She *surfed* the net until two in the morning.
He has been *surfing* real estate listings all week.

gloss: To save a picture of what is on your screen.
examples: *Screenshot* the confirmation page.
She *screenshotted* the whole conversation.
He is *screenshotting* every message as proof.
contrast: Double the t: screenshotted, screenshotting. In formal writing, take a screenshot is safer.

gloss: To give something a score or a number of stars.
examples: Please *rate* the driver after the ride.
She *rated* the app one star.
The movie has been *rated* by forty thousand people.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: rating.

transitivity: both — transitive (the algorithm ranks the results), intransitive (the site ranks first)
gloss: To put items in order by importance, or to hold a place in such an order.
examples: Search engines *rank* pages by hundreds of signals.
The site *ranked* third for that keyword.
The app is *ranking* higher every month.

gloss: To warn someone about something quickly.
examples: The app will *alert* you when the price drops.
The system *alerted* the whole team at 3 a.m.
It has been *alerting* us every hour since then.
contrast: You alert someone TO a problem.

gloss: To ask a user on screen to do something, or to give a system an instruction.
examples: The site will *prompt* you for a code.
It *prompted* me to change my password.
The app keeps *prompting* me to rate it.
contrast: Prompt someone TO do something, or prompt someone FOR information.

gloss: To act on each other, or to communicate with a person or a system.
examples: Children *interact* with screens before they can read.
The two programs *interacted* badly and the system froze.
He has been *interacting* with customers all day.
contrast: You interact WITH someone or something.

gloss: To be able to work with a device, a format, or a feature.
examples: The old phone does not *support* the new app.
They *supported* that file format until last year.
The browser has *supported* it since 2020.

gloss: To settle a problem or an error so that it stops happening.
examples: Rebooting will usually *resolve* it.
Support *resolved* the ticket in ten minutes.
They are still *resolving* the outage.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: resolving.

gloss: To fail or behave strangely for a short time.
examples: Cheap screens *glitch* in the cold.
The payment page *glitched* and charged me twice.
The video keeps *glitching* at the same spot.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: glitches.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sun overheated the phone), intransitive (the laptop overheats)
gloss: To become, or to make something become, too hot to work safely.
examples: Old laptops *overheat* under any real load.
The phone *overheated* in the car.
The battery is *overheating* again.

gloss: To make a disk or a drive come out safely.
examples: *Eject* the drive before you pull it out.
He *ejected* the card and the photos were gone.
The laptop is *ejecting* the disc.

gloss: To separate one part or file from another.
examples: You can *detach* the keyboard and use the screen as a tablet.
She *detached* the file and sent the note alone.
He is *detaching* the cables one at a time.
contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: detaches. You detach one thing FROM another.

gloss: To break the connection between two accounts, files, or devices.
examples: *Unlink* the card before you close the account.
He *unlinked* his email from the old profile.
She has *unlinked* every app from her calendar.

gloss: To play a recording or a game again.
examples: *Replay* the last ten seconds.
They *replayed* the clip in slow motion.
He is *replaying* the level for the fifth time.
contrast: The verb is ree-PLAY; the noun replay is REE-play. The -y follows a vowel, so it does not change: replayed.

transitivity: both — transitive (shuffle the playlist), intransitive (the app shuffles automatically)
gloss: To put songs, cards, or files into a random order.
examples: *Shuffle* the playlist - I know it by heart.
The app *shuffled* the same five songs all night.
It is *shuffling* my whole library.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: shuffling.

ru: объединять в сеть, объединить в сеть
transitivity: both — transitive (network the office printers), intransitive (the machines network over Wi-Fi)
gloss: To connect computers or devices so that they can share data.
examples: We can *network* all four printers.
They *networked* the two offices last year.
Every machine is *networked* through one switch.
